strengths: Comprehensive, well-executed empirical study: 14 explanation methods spanning gradient-, propagation-, perturbation-, and attention-based families, evaluated on both encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only (Llama3.2, Qwen3) models, two hate speech datasets, three bias types, and multiple traditional debiasing baselines — this breadth is significantly beyond prior mostly qualitative work.

Clearly structured around three practically motivated research questions, with nuanced and useful findings: explanations help detect biased predictions (RQ1) and aid bias mitigation during training (RQ3), but are unreliable for model selection (RQ2) — a valuable negative result with practical guidance.

Good methodological hygiene: statistical significance checks on fairness correlations, multiple random validation splits for model selection, results averaged over runs, and a fairness-accuracy harmonic mean for balanced comparison; the fairness-based hyperparameter tuning strategy is a sensible improvement over prior work (Dimanov et al., 2020).

Additional analyses strengthen the contribution: showing bias detection survives explanation-based debiasing, demonstrating that LLM self-reflection/self-attribution are poor bias detectors compared to attribution-based approaches, and showing faithfulness is not a predictor of bias-detection utility — all practically relevant for practitioners choosing explanation methods.
Reproducibility: full implementation details, prompts, data splits, hyperparameters, and code submitted as supplementary material, with a commitment to open-source release.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the individual components (attribution-based bias detection, explanation-regularized debiasing following Dimanov et al., 2020, validation-set fairness as a selection baseline) are largely established techniques; the main contribution is a systematic aggregation and evaluation rather than a new method or insight, which limits impact beyond the hate speech detection sub-area.

Scope limitations undermine the 'first comprehensive study' framing: only binary hate speech classification with two related datasets (Civil Comments and Jigsaw, both toxicity corpora with partially overlapping design), and identity terms limited to a predefined vocabulary for race/gender/religion; generalization to other tasks, domains, and identity groups is uncertain (acknowledged in the ethics statement but not empirically explored).

The individual unfairness metric depends on counterfactual group substitution via token replacement, which is sensitive to the quality of sensitive-token vocabularies and may not capture more subtle or contextual forms of bias; correlations between attribution scores and this metric could partially reflect metric artifacts rather than genuine bias detection.

RQ2 (model selection) is evaluated over a small pool of candidate models (7 encoder, 4 decoder), which limits the statistical power of rank correlation and MRR@1 comparisons; conclusions of unreliability may not hold with larger candidate sets.

Some findings are confirmatory rather than surprising (e.g., perturbation/occlusion-based methods detecting reliance on identity terms), and the paper would benefit from more discussion of when and why the effective methods (Occlusion, L2-based) succeed versus fail, beyond the direction-vs-magnitude intuition.

Results presentation is dense: many results relegated to appendices, and key comparisons (e.g., Figure 4 mitigation results) are hard to read; quantitative tables for the main mitigation results would improve clarity and verifiability.

strengths: The paper is a broad and well-organized empirical study connecting input-based explanations and fairness, covering 14 post-hoc explanation methods, encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only (Llama3.2, Qwen3) models, two hate speech datasets, three bias types, and multiple traditional debiasing baselines.

The three-RQ decomposition (bias detection, model selection, bias mitigation) is a sensible framing, and the mixed findings are reported honestly rather than oversold: explanations help detection/mitigation but fail for model selection.

Useful secondary analyses, including the study of bias detection in explanation-debiased models, the comparison against LLM-as-a-Judge (self-reflection and self-attribution), and the finding that explanation faithfulness does not predict bias detection ability (Appendix G).
Reproducibility appears reasonable: implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, split sizes, and code/config files as supplementary material are provided, and an ethics statement is included.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Each component closely follows prior work: explanation-regularized debiasing is essentially Dimanov et al. (2020) and Kennedy et al. (2020) adapted to hate speech, and the detection analysis follows Meng et al. (2022) and Sogancioglu et al. (2023). The main contribution is breadth of quantification rather than a new method or insight, which weakens the fit for a top-tier venue. The repeated claim of being the 'first comprehensive quantitative study' is overstated given prior quantitative work (e.g., Balkir et al., 2022).

Scope is narrow and generalization is uncertain. All conclusions rest on two English hate speech datasets, binary toxicity labels, three bias types (race/gender/religion), and small data subsets (8K training examples per bias type). The authors acknowledge this, but it substantially limits the significance of the headline claims ('input-based explanations can/cannot do X') for fairness in NLP more broadly.

Methodological concerns in the core evaluation: (1) the 'sensitive token reliance' score takes only the max absolute attribution over sensitive tokens, and results are sensitive to this and other design choices (raw vs. normalized scores are chosen post hoc based on best results, per footnote 1); (2) individual unfairness relies on counterfactual group substitutions that may produce unnatural text; (3) the fairness-correlation methodology in RQ1 averages absolute Pearson correlations across class-group pairs, which can mask sign inconsistency and be driven by token-frequency artifacts.

The RQ2 (model selection) analysis is underpowered and possibly invalid: rank correlations are computed over only 11 encoder-only or 4 decoder-only candidate models, where a Spearman correlation or MRR@1 over 4 models is extremely noisy, and a 'perfect rank correlation of 1' for the decoder-only baseline is more likely an artifact of the tiny candidate pool than a meaningful result. Negative conclusions drawn from such small candidate sets are fragile.

Evidence for RQ3 is mixed and selectively presented in the main text. The main figures highlight models 'with the highest average AvgIU' and single-bias-type training; the mitigation gains are inconsistent across fairness metrics (e.g., reductions in Disp_fnr coexist with increases or no change on other metrics), and the fairness-based hyperparameter tuning makes the comparison with Dimanov et al. not apples-to-apples. The claim of 'effective bias mitigation with a good fairness-performance trade-off' is stronger than the mixed results support.

Presentation choices weaken the main-text evidence: many key results (RoBERTa, Llama3.2, Jigsaw, religion bias, additional debiasing setups) are relegated to dense appendix figures (up to 27), making it hard to verify that the main-text takeaways hold uniformly; several figures (e.g., Figures 4, 18-21) are visually cluttered and difficult to interpret.

The LLM-as-a-Judge comparison (Section 6) uses only Qwen3 and simple prompt-based self-reflection/self-attribution baselines, so the conclusion that explanations 'outperform LLM judgments' is limited to one weak setup rather than a general finding.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap: the first systematic, large-scale quantitative study of the relationship between input-based explanations and fairness in NLP, whereas prior work (e.g., Balkir et al. 2022, Deck et al. 2024) is largely qualitative or limited in scope.

Well-structured around three concrete research questions (bias detection, fair model selection, bias mitigation), each with a clearly stated takeaway, which makes the contributions easy to follow and actionable for practitioners.

Comprehensive empirical coverage: 14 variants of explanation methods spanning four methodological families, encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only (Llama3.2, Qwen3) models, two datasets, three bias types, and multiple existing debiasing baselines.

The negative result for RQ2 (explanations are unreliable for model selection) is valuable and honestly reported, and the paper explains the divergence between RQ1 and RQ2 results with a plausible mechanism.

Useful additional analyses: (a) comparison against LLM-as-a-judge bias detection (self-reflection and self-attribution), showing explanations outperform LLM judgments; (b) testing robustness of bias detection in explanation-debiased models; (c) a faithfulness analysis showing faithfulness does not predict bias-detection ability — an important methodological insight.

Reasonable statistical rigor in RQ1 (per class-group significance testing) and averaging over multiple random validation splits and training runs in RQ2/RQ3; code submitted as supplementary material with a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the technical methods: the RQ3 debiasing objective is directly adopted from Dimanov et al. (2020), and the core finding that suppressing sensitive-token attributions helps is largely confirmatory; the contribution is primarily an empirical audit rather than a new method or theory.

Narrow scope limits generality: only two datasets, both Jigsaw-family toxicity corpora (Civil Comments and Jigsaw), binary classification, three predefined bias types, and four models; the paper's claims about explainability and fairness may not transfer to other tasks or bias settings, as acknowledged in the ethics statement.

Potential confound in the RQ1 metric: sensitive token reliance may correlate with identity mentions and content toxicity rather than with 'bias' per se; the Pearson correlation with individual unfairness does not establish that explanations detect bias rather than simply identity-bearing text. A more careful causal/controlled analysis would strengthen the claim.

Correlation magnitudes are only moderate (roughly 0.3-0.6) and the fairness-correlation methodology (averaging absolute correlations across class-group pairs) may mask sign inconsistencies; correlation-based evidence alone leaves open practical usefulness questions that are not quantified (e.g., precision/recall of flagging biased predictions at chosen thresholds, except briefly in Section 6).

Decoder-only analysis is comparatively thin: only prompting-based debiasing (no fine-tuning), reliance on a single instruction style, and explanation methods applied to generative models without deep discussion of their validity in that setting.

Some presentation issues: main figures (Figures 1, 2, 4) are dense and hard to read; key results rely heavily on appendix material; several text fragments appear misplaced or duplicated in Section 5 (e.g., a sentence about Qwen3 appears inside the BERT analysis).

Ablations on the choice of the reliance-score aggregation (max absolute value, footnote 1) and on α selection sensitivity in RQ3 are minimal, raising questions about robustness of the reported conclusions to these design choices.

strengths: First large-scale, systematic quantitative study of the relationship between input-based explanations and fairness in NLP, addressing a real gap since prior work (Balkir et al., 2022; Deck et al., 2024) is mostly qualitative; the three-RQ framing (detection, selection, mitigation) is well motivated and clearly structured.

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation: 16 explanation methods across methodological families, encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only (Llama3.2, Qwen3) models, two hate speech datasets, both group and individual fairness metrics, with statistical significance checks for fairness correlations.

Balanced and honest reporting of negative results (RQ2: explanations fail as automatic fair-model selectors), which is valuable and less common in the literature; the contrast between RQ1 and RQ2 is analyzed rather than glossed over.

Strong breadth of supporting analyses: faithfulness vs. bias-detection ability (Appendix I), human fairness auditing study (Appendix J), LLM-as-a-judge comparison (Section 6), explanation-debiased model probing (Section 5), hybrid debiasing (Appendix K), and generalization tests across tasks, alignment types, and vocabulary coverage (Appendix H).

Practical takeaways for practitioners (e.g., Occlusion- and L2-based methods for detection; IxG L2 and attention-based methods for mitigation), plus computational cost analysis (Appendix C) and detailed reproducibility information.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core mechanisms (sensitive token reliance from Dimanov et al., 2020; the Ldebias regularizer) are adopted rather than introduced, making this primarily an empirical benchmarking study; the 'first comprehensive quantitative analysis' claim is somewhat overstated given prior quantitative efforts (e.g., Meng et al., 2022).

The main evaluation metric (Pearson correlation between sensitive token reliance and individual unfairness) is a relatively blunt instrument; correlations of ~0.4–0.6 are moderate, and no task-level detection metrics (e.g., precision/recall of flagging biased predictions at realistic flagging rates) are reported beyond a single 'Grad L2 Binary' baseline in the LLM comparison.

Main-text results are restricted to BERT and Qwen3-4B on single-bias-type training; while appendices extend coverage, several key conclusions rest on these limited setups, and the individual unfairness metric via counterfactual group substitution may conflate bias with legitimate lexical/semantic sensitivity.

Some findings are confirmatory rather than surprising (explanations reflect sensitive-token reliance but don't rank models; debiasing regularization reduces reliance), which weakens the sense of significant new insight beyond systematization.

A few presentation and rigor gaps: the code availability URL is missing in the abstract/reproducibility statement; RQ3 lacks error bars in the main figures despite three-run averaging; the LLM-as-a-judge comparison (Table 2) covers only one model's predictions on one bias subset, limiting that conclusion's generality.

strengths: The paper is the first large-scale, quantitative study of the relationship between input-based explanations and fairness in NLP, moving beyond the predominantly qualitative analyses in prior work; this is a genuinely useful empirical contribution to the fair-XAI literature.

The experimental scope is broad and systematically designed: 16 explanation methods spanning gradient-, propagation-, perturbation-, and attention-based families, multiple encoder- and decoder-only models (BERT, RoBERTa, Llama3.2, Qwen3-4B/8B), two datasets, three bias types, and both default and debiased model configurations.

The three research questions (bias detection, model selection, bias mitigation) are well-motivated and cover the main use cases proposed for explanations in fairness auditing, including the practically relevant negative result that explanations are unreliable for model selection (RQ2).

Useful auxiliary analyses: faithfulness is shown not to predict bias-detection ability (Appendix I), a human study probes explanation-assisted auditing (Appendix J), LLM-as-a-judge is compared against attribution-based detection (Section 6), and generalization checks across tasks, alignment types, and reduced sensitive-token vocabularies are provided (Appendix H).
The paper is generally well organized with clear takeaways, hyperparameter/implementation details, computational cost reporting, and a code release, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: all metrics, explanation methods, and the core debiasing regularization (following Dimanov et al., 2020) are existing components; the contribution is essentially a large benchmark/empirical evaluation. The RQ3 setup closely replicates prior explanation-regularization work, with the main delta being a fairness-based hyperparameter tuning strategy. 'First comprehensive quantitative study' overstates novelty given prior surveys and semi-quantitative studies (Balkir et al., 2022; Deck et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2022).

The headline positive finding (RQ1) is close to tautological: individual unfairness is defined via counterfactual group substitution, so a model whose predictions change under substitution will naturally place attribution mass on the very sensitive tokens that define the counterfactual. The paper does not sufficiently discuss this potential circularity between the sensitive-token reliance score and the IU metric, nor does it control for the alternative explanation that L2/Occlusion methods detect bias simply because any explanation that flags identity terms correlates with counterfactual sensitivity.

Statistical rigor around the main RQ1 metric is thin: fairness correlations are averaged across class–group pairs with no confidence intervals or effect-size discussion, and the repeated train/test sampling procedures for fairness metrics are not validated for stability. Multiple comparisons across 16 methods are not corrected for.

Significance of conclusions is modest: that L2/occlusion-style explanations flag identity terms, that explanation-based model selection underperforms direct validation-set fairness evaluation, and that penalizing identity-term attribution during training reduces Dispfnr are all fairly predictable outcomes. Practical impact is further limited by the authors' own admission that no single method consistently wins (Appendix M), so the paper cannot offer actionable selection guidance.

Scope limitations are substantial for the claims made: only hate speech detection (sentiment is a small appendix check), only two datasets with small sampled subsets (8k training examples per bias type), and group fairness receives much shallower treatment than individual fairness (the RQ2 analysis itself notes explanation metrics and validation-set fairness both fail beyond chance for group metrics, which is glossed over in the narrative).

Some experimental choices lack justification: excluding reasoning models/CoT from the decoder analysis, using [PAD] tokens for perturbation faithfulness in Qwen3-4B, deriving sensitive vocabularies from external resources, and excluding slur-based examples (which may distort the bias being measured) are all consequential but under-argued.

Presentation issues: several figures (e.g., Figures 2, 5, 7-10) are dense and hard to parse; Table 1 aggregates three bias types per cell making trends hard to read; there are typos ('sp we apply', 'they outperforms'); and key details are deferred to an appendix that is nearly four times the length of the main text.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-structured empirical study: the paper systematically addresses three clearly framed research questions (bias detection, model selection, bias mitigation) across 16 explanation methods, encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only (Llama3.2, Qwen3) models, two hate speech datasets, and multiple debiasing baselines—an unusually broad experimental scope for this topic.

Useful and actionable findings: the results give practical guidance to practitioners—Occlusion- and L2-based methods work well for bias detection, explanation-based debiasing yields a good fairness-accuracy trade-off, but explanation-based model selection is unreliable (a valuable negative result), and explanation faithfulness does not predict bias-detection ability.

Beyond the three RQs, the paper adds several strong supplementary analyses: comparison against LLM-as-a-judge (showing explanations outperform it), a study of bias detection in explanation-debiased models (addressing the 'hiding bias from explanations' concern), a small human study on explanation-assisted auditing, faithfulness-vs-fairness-correlation analysis, hybrid debiasing, and generalization tests to another task, other alignment types, and reduced sensitive vocabularies.
Good reproducibility: implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, computational costs, and code availability are provided; statistical significance of correlations is reported.
Well written overall, with clear takeaways per section and honest limitations discussion (Appendix M, ethics statement).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the contribution is an empirical evaluation rather than a new technique; the debiasing objective in RQ3 closely follows Dimanov et al. (2020) (differing mainly in the hyperparameter selection criterion), and many findings qualitatively confirm what prior qualitative work already suggested (e.g., explanations reveal reliance on sensitive features; model selection is unreliable). The 'first systematic/quantitative study' claim is somewhat overstated given Meng et al. (2022) and related work.

Potential circularity in the core RQ1 metric: sensitive token reliance (attributions on identity tokens) and individual unfairness (prediction change under group substitution) are both driven by the same underlying phenomenon—model sensitivity to identity tokens. A positive correlation may be partly expected by construction, and the paper could more carefully discuss whether the correlation reflects genuinely new detection ability or a near-tautological relationship.

The scope is largely restricted to hate speech detection with a specific sensitive-token-vocabulary-based notion of bias (binary counterfactual swaps of a small set of identity terms); the group fairness analysis is thinner than the individual fairness analysis, and generalization beyond Civil Comments/Jigsaw is only preliminary (Appendix H).

Some experimental choices are under-justified or thin: the human study involves only 6 annotators and 48 examples; the RQ2 conclusion rests on one explanation-based metric and may not rule out other aggregation strategies (acknowledged by the authors); encoder models trained on relatively small subsets (8k examples) may not reflect production-scale behavior.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('sp we apply', 'they outperforms'), Figure 2/5 are dense and hard to read, and the RQ3 mitigation experiments are restricted to single bias types for computational reasons, limiting direct comparison with the multi-bias settings of RQ1/RQ2.
